newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian Senate opens door a crack to extradition.
newsitem.headline: Colombian Senate opens door a crack to extradition.

text.p: A Senate panel approved a controversial constitutional reform bill on Tuesday that would partially lift Colombia's 6-year-old ban on the extradition of drug traffickers and other criminals.

But the bill, approved by the constitutional affairs committee of the Senate, faces more legislative hurdles before it can become law and was so watered down that some lawmakers said it was essentially useless.

Critics conceded that it opened the door to extradition, if only a crack. But they stressed that it also ruled out the practice in cases where criminals would face stiffer penalities abroad than at home -- or in the case of criminals who give themselves up before they are caught.

The bill would effectively block extradition of any major drug lord to the United States since Colombia's maximum penalty for trafficking is 60 years, whereas life sentences have been handed down by U.S. judges for the same crime.

"It leaves it up to the drug trafficker to determine whether or not he'll be extradited," Sen. Luis Guillermo Giraldo, a leading proponent of extradition, jokingly told reporters after the committee vote.
"It's no good for Colombia or for the international community," added Claudia Blum, a fellow commiteee member representing the opposition New Democratic Force.

The government had proposed that lawmakers simply abrogate Article 35 of the constitution -- the one banning the extradition of any Colombian nationals -- and let Colombia's pre-existing extradition treaties determine when, and where, Colombian criminals would face justice abroad.

But two ruling party lawmakers drafted a separate bill with the pre-conditions that were approved on Tuesday. The vote followed hours of debate in which Washington was accused by many, including Interior Minister Horacio Serpa, of meddling in Colombia's internal affairs and applying undue pressure in favour of extradition.

Serpa, a firebrand populist who gave a 50-minute speech urging lawmkers to lift the extradition ban, noted that he himself had voted in favour of the ban in 1991. He stressed that support for ending it did not mean that anyone was "an unconditional lackey of the United States."

But Serpa has had frequent clashes with Washington on drug policy and other matters, and his speech appeared to be aimed at scoring political points as much as it did with winning the fight to revive a practice polls show most Colombians oppose. It was perhaps no coincidence that he used his speech to defend himself from new drug corruption allegations and to announce that he intends to step down within days to launch a campaign for the presidency.
Despite its flaws, Giraldo said passage of the bill marked a certain victory, since it could encourage drug lords to surrender rather than face possible extradition.

Constitutional reforms must be approved by two consecutive sessions of Congress. The current sessions ends on June 20, and the bill must be approved by the full Senate and the lower House of Representatives, before being passed on to the next session of Congress that will be installed on July 20.
